tasks.mathematicsAndAnswers: IMPRESSION has ten letters, with two I and two S. Choose five positions for the unique ordered P,R,E,S,S subsequence and arrange O,N,I,M,I in the remainder: C(10,5)5!/2! = 10!/(5!2!) = 15120, option B. There is exactly one representation per valid word because there are exactly two S; no overcount from the repeated S.

tasks.mathematicsAndAnswers: Under independent uniform draws, part a is the product of probabilities of k distinct first draws and a repeat on the next. Part b holds precisely on its natural comparison domain 2 <= k <= n: P(k)/P(k-1)=k(n-k+1)/(n(k-1)), so the inequality is equivalent to k^2-k-n <= 0. At k=1 the question defines P(1) but not P(0), so its comparison is undefined; do not invent P(0). Part c is valid since k >= 1 makes k-1/2 positive and integer n > k(k-1) gives n >= k(k-1)+1 > (k-1/2)^2. Part d conclusion is correct under the probability model, but the current solution incorrectly claims part b alone supplies a converse and assumes a global maximum from a local comparison without establishing monotonicity or treating the endpoint.

requiredEdits.prescription: State in the explanation that the displayed formula follows under independent uniform selections. Flag the unexpressed probability model as a source ambiguity for an explicit decision; do not silently add it to the posed givens. Explain the first k draws are distinct and the next repeats one of them.

Retain the source prompt and all four parts. Explicitly state that P(k-1) is defined only for 2 <= k <= n, and derive the displayed inequality there by the positive ratio P(k)/P(k-1)=k(n-k+1)/(n(k-1)); the algebra gives an equivalence. Note that at k=1 the comparison is undefined, without assigning P(0).

Replace the opening assertion with a complete discrete-mode proof: for 2 <= k <= n, the ratio is greater than 1 exactly when k^2-k-n < 0 and less than 1 exactly when it is > 0. Under 4n+1 nonsquare the positive root r=1/2+sqrt(n+1/4) is nonintegral, hence ratios are strictly above 1 for integer k<r and strictly below 1 for k>r. Here n=2 is excluded because 4n+1=9; for n>=3, 2<r<n, so the sequence increases from P(1) to P(floor r) and decreases thereafter. Thus the unique mode is floor r. Part c and the immediate converse show, for integer k>=1, k<r iff k-1/2<sqrt(n), so floor r is the greatest integer below sqrt(n)+1/2, the unique closest integer to sqrt(n). This uses P(1) as the starting endpoint and never P(0).
